name: blake2b_simd / blake2s_simd
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-512 / OpenSSL SHA-1 (also compared to libsodium BLAKE2b)
workload: Hashing long inputs in memory, averaged over many runs (benches/bench_multiprocess), comparing BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s AVX2 SIMD implementations against native OpenSSL and libsodium hash functions via FFI
claimed_speedup: blake2b_simd BLAKE2b: 2.81 cpb vs OpenSSL SHA-512: 5.11 cpb (~1.8x); vs OpenSSL SHA-1: 3.51 cpb (~1.25x); vs libsodium BLAKE2b: 3.07 cpb (~1.09x). blake2s_simd many::hash: 1.31 cpb, blake2b_simd many::hash: 1.43 cpb
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with dynamic AVX2 CPU-feature detection at runtime; SIMD kernel is a Rust port of Samuel Neves' sneves/blake2-avx2 C code. Not C++-native (usable from C++ only via FFI/cbindgen), no_std support optional. Benchmark numbers are from 2019-2020 hardware (i5-8250U, OpenSSL 1.1.1d), so absolute cycles/byte on current CPUs/OpenSSL 3.x will differ, though the relative BLAKE2b-vs-SHA-512 gap is architectural and should persist.
caveats: Benchmark table is several years old (OpenSSL 1.1.1d, rustc 1.40.0) and was run on the author's own laptop rather than a dedicated benchmark server; comparison against libsodium BLAKE2b (same algorithm) is a much smaller win (~9%) than against OpenSSL SHA-512 (different algorithm family, ~1.8x), so the headline number depends heavily on which baseline is emphasized.
found_via: crates.io API query q=blake2 -> blake2b_simd/blake2s_simd crate description 'a pure Rust BLAKE2b implementation with dynamic SIMD', then opened linked GitHub repo README

name: keccak-batch
baseline: keccak-asm (assembly Keccak-256 backend behind Alloy's asm-keccak feature) and tiny-keccak scalar implementation
workload: Batched Keccak-256 hashing of 64-byte inputs (Merkle/BMT-node hot path) and 4 KiB inputs, comparing SIMD-batched (SSE2/NEON/wasm, AVX2, AVX-512) lane widths against the crate's own scalar path and against keccak-asm/tiny-keccak, via `cargo run --release --example perf`
claimed_speedup: 8-wide AVX-512 batch: ~5.4x (64-byte) / ~4-5x (4 KiB) over own scalar path; scalar path is at parity with tiny-keccak; keccak-asm is ~1.3x faster than scalar; 8-wide batch is still ~5.5x faster per hash than keccak-asm
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release --example perf; KECCAK_BATCH_NO_AVX512 / KECCAK_BATCH_NO_AVX2 env flags to cap backend
hardware: "Zen-class AVX-512 part" (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Pre-release (marked pre-release in repo badge), only implements legacy 0x01-padding Keccak-256 (not full SHA3-256 with 0x06 padding), AGPL-3.0 copyleft license restricts embedding in proprietary C++ code without a compatible C API wrapper, no C/C++ bindings provided (Rust crate only, though a cdylib could be built).
caveats: Very new (created 2026-09-24), essentially a single-author, 1-star, pre-release project; benchmark hardware is described only as "a Zen-class AVX-512 part" rather than an exact CPU model, and baseline is the crate's own scalar implementation plus two other Rust crates rather than OpenSSL/XKCP directly, so this falls short of Tier A/B. Numbers are self-reported with partial methodology.
found_via: crates.io API query q=keccak avx -> keccak-batch crate description 'Batched Keccak-256 (legacy 0x01 padding) with runtime-dispatched SIMD', then opened linked GitHub repo README

name: Intel Cryptography Primitives Library
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-2/SHA-3 (generic implementation, no CPU-specific dispatch)
workload: No benchmark numbers published in the repository; README/OVERVIEW.md only describe runtime CPU dispatching (SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512/AVX10.2 code paths) for SHA-1/224/256/384/512, SHA3-224/256/384/512, SHAKE128/256, MD5, SM3 and other primitives, marketed as 'a secure, fast and lightweight library ... highly-optimized for various Intel CPUs'
claimed_speedup: unquantified ("fast and lightweight", CPU-specific optimized code paths incl. SHA-NI); no numbers found in README, OVERVIEW.md, or BUILD.md
stars_or_usage: 388 stars; formerly Intel IPP Cryptography (intel/ipp-crypto), FIPS 140-3 validated, used across Intel's oneAPI/toolchain ecosystem
tradeoffs: C API with a runtime CPU-feature dispatcher (multiple codepaths compiled in, best one selected at init); large surface area beyond just hashing (AES, RSA, ECC, PQC, etc.); Intel-specific tuning means gains are concentrated on Intel CPUs with AVX-512/SHA-NI, may not help on AMD or older hardware.
caveats: No first-party benchmark numbers found anywhere in the repo despite extensive searching (README, OVERVIEW.md, BUILD.md); the 'fast' claim is unquantified marketing language. Included only as a single Tier-D entry per the rules because the project is Intel-authored, FIPS-validated, and widely referenced in Intel's own crypto tooling. Rename from intel/ipp-crypto to intel/cryptography-primitives should be tracked so it isn't confused with a different project.
found_via: gh search repos 'sha256 sha-ni intrinsics' surfaced Intel SHA-NI discussion; direct lookup of gh api repos/intel/ipp-crypto redirected to intel/cryptography-primitives
